content: I started the year by writing down what I want from my career over the next two years. I want to become a stronger software engineer rather than simply collecting more framework names. My main technical goals are system design, cloud infrastructure, backend engineering, and practical AI application development. I also want to become more comfortable explaining trade-offs in interviews. A recurring problem in my learning is that I read about many subjects without building enough things. I am changing that by attaching each major topic to a project. For example, I want to learn retrieval-augmented generation by building a private journal assistant. The project should let me ask questions about old entries, retrieve relevant passages, and show the evidence used for an answer. I wrote down this plan because I want to be able to look back later and see whether my actual work matched my intentions.

My mornings have been inconsistent, especially on days when I work late the previous evening. I experimented with preparing everything the night before: clothes, water bottle, breakfast ingredients, and a short list of priorities. The small amount of preparation made getting started easier. I also decided not to check social media immediately after waking up. Instead, I spend the first few minutes reviewing the day's calendar and deciding what absolutely needs attention. This is not a rigid productivity system. I mainly want fewer decisions before I become fully alert. I noticed that when I start calmly, I am less likely to spend the first hour reacting to messages. I want to keep this routine for several weeks before deciding whether it is actually useful.

I reviewed the architecture of a web application I have been working with and tried to understand it as a set of responsibilities rather than a collection of folders. The frontend handles presentation and interaction, the API coordinates business operations, repositories manage persistence, and background workers handle tasks that do not need to block a request. Thinking this way made several design decisions easier to explain. I also noticed areas where boundaries are not clean and a change in one layer often requires changes elsewhere. I wrote down examples of coupling so I can discuss them later when studying refactoring. One important lesson is that architecture is not about creating as many layers as possible. Every abstraction should have a reason, and the cost of indirection should be justified by the problem it solves.

I finished a book about habits and wrote a summary immediately afterward. The idea that stayed with me was that changing the environment can be more reliable than depending on motivation. I applied that idea to technical learning by leaving my notebook open on the desk and keeping a small list of questions next to the computer. I also started making shorter reading notes. Instead of trying to capture every interesting sentence, I record the main argument, one example, and whether I think the idea is applicable to my own work. This should make the notes more useful for future retrieval. I am beginning to think of my personal notes as a searchable knowledge base rather than a collection of forgotten documents.

I began a simple exercise routine with three strength sessions and several walking days each week. My goal is consistency rather than an aggressive target. I noticed that exercise affects my evening study sessions more than I expected. On days when I take a walk after work, I transition out of work mode more easily and can concentrate on learning afterward. I am also trying to avoid treating missed sessions as failures. If something interrupts the plan, I want to resume at the next reasonable opportunity instead of abandoning the whole week. I wrote down this approach because I tend to over-plan routines and then become frustrated when real life changes them.
